question: Does Obeka, Brute Chronologist's ability go on the stack and can it be responded to?
expected_answer: Yes to both. It is an activated ability that is not a mana ability, so it is put on the stack when activated and the activator gets priority afterward; other players can respond before it resolves. When it resolves, the player whose turn it is (not necessarily Obeka's controller) may choose to end the turn, which follows the special procedure in 724.1.
notes: Tests that the answer notices 'the player whose turn it is' decides, and that ending the turn exiles the stack including the resolving ability. Draft expectations: not yet reviewed.

question: What happens when you clone Princess Yue with a card like Clever Impersonator?
expected_answer: Clever Impersonator enters as a copy of Princess Yue, so you control two legendary permanents named Princess Yue and the legend rule makes you choose one and put the other into the graveyard. If the Clever Impersonator copy goes to the graveyard, it dies and Princess Yue's trigger returns that card (Clever Impersonator) to the battlefield tapped as a land named Moon with '{T}: Add {C}'. As it re-enters, its 'may enter as a copy of any nonland permanent' replacement effect applies again, so you may copy another nonland permanent; the result has the copied permanent's abilities but is a land named Moon that can tap for colorless. (If you instead put the original Princess Yue into the graveyard, she returns as Moon and the Clever Impersonator copy stays on the battlefield as a creature.)
notes: Answer supplied by the user; wording adjusted by Claude in two places, please confirm: (1) the legend rule puts permanents into the graveyard, it does not sacrifice them (704.5j). (2) Clever Impersonator's copy choice is a replacement effect (614.1c, choice made before entering per 614.12a), not an enters-the-battlefield trigger. Not located in the CR text: an explicit rule for which layer a 'named Moon' name-setting effect applies in relative to the copy effect (layer 1a, 613.2a), so the 'name will be Moon on the copy' detail rests on your reasoning or a ruling, not a rule I could cite.

question: When a non-permanent spell is resolved after being cast from exile, where does the card go?
expected_answer: It goes to its owner's graveyard as the final part of its resolution (608.2n). Where the spell was cast from doesn't change this, and it is the owner's graveyard even if someone else cast it. The exception is an effect that specifically says otherwise. For example, a rebound spell is exiled instead of going to the graveyard only if it was cast from hand (702.88a), so when you cast it from exile on the next upkeep it goes to the graveyard.
notes: Rewritten from a broader question. Checks that the answer states the owner's graveyard and does not invent an exile or battlefield destination just because the card was cast from exile. Rebound is the natural counter-example: rebound only applies to spells cast from hand. An earlier draft wrongly used flashback as the exception, but flashback casts from the graveyard, so it isn't relevant. Draft expectations: not yet reviewed.

question: What happens when Humility is returned as a creature with Anikthea, Hand of Erebos?
expected_answer: Anikthea's trigger creates a token copy of Humility that is also a 3/3 black Zombie creature. Humility's effect then applies to every creature, including its own token copy and Anikthea: in layer 6 they all lose all abilities, and in layer 7b they all have base power and toughness 1/1, overriding the token's copied 3/3. Humility losing its own ability doesn't stop the effect: once an effect has started to apply in one layer it keeps applying to the same objects in the other layers even if the ability generating it is removed (613.6). So the token and every other creature, Anikthea included, are 1/1 with no abilities.
notes: Answer supplied by the user; supporting rules found by Claude in the CR text. The Humility rulings dated 2009-10-01 describe the same 'keeps applying after the ability is lost' principle using Opalescence. Unlike those cases, no timestamp or dependency is needed here because the 3/3 is a copiable value set in layer 1 (see the 2023-07-28 Anikthea ruling), and Humility's effects apply in later layers. Details added by Claude, please confirm: the token stays a black Zombie enchantment creature (Humility doesn't change types or colors), Anikthea herself loses menace and her triggers, and the trigger that already created the token is unaffected because a triggered ability on the stack exists independently of its source (113.7a).

question: Which creatures are destroyed at the end step when both Silent Arbiter and Season of the Witch are in play?
expected_answer: Season of the Witch destroys every untapped creature that didn't attack this turn, except creatures that couldn't attack. Silent Arbiter only limits how many creatures can be declared as attackers together; it doesn't stop any individual creature from being the one declared. So every untapped creature the active player controls that could have attacked (it has haste or has been controlled continuously since the turn began) is destroyed unless it was the single creature that attacked. That includes Silent Arbiter itself if it didn't attack. Creatures with summoning sickness, tapped creatures, and creatures controlled by players other than the active player (which couldn't attack this turn) are not destroyed.
notes: Answer supplied by the user; Claude added three refinements, please confirm: (1) only the active player's creatures could have attacked, so other players' creatures survive; (2) tapped creatures survive because the card says untapped; (3) Silent Arbiter is itself a creature and is destroyed if it didn't attack. Key card ruling the answer should use: Season of the Witch 2013-09-20 ('every creature that could have been declared as an attacker ... but wasn't will be destroyed' and a summoning-sick creature isn't destroyed). Neither a rule nor a ruling addresses this exact pairing. The conclusion is an inference: 508.1c treats restrictions as checks on the whole declaration (its example is 'can't attack alone', where declaring both is legal), so Silent Arbiter's limit doesn't make any one creature unable to attack, only unable to attack together with another. If you have an official source for this pairing, add it.

question: If Golgari Grave-Troll is the only creature in your graveyard when you cast Reanimate on it, how many +1/+1 counters will it enter with?
expected_answer: One counter. Golgari Grave-Troll's 'enters with a +1/+1 counter for each creature card in your graveyard' is a replacement effect (614.1c) that applies as it enters the battlefield, while the Troll is still in the graveyard, so it counts itself (official ruling, 2018-12-07). The count is determined when the effect is applied, as Reanimate resolves, not when Reanimate was cast (608.2h, 614.1). If another creature card were put into your graveyard in response to Reanimate, the Troll would enter with 2 counters.
notes: The number (1) was supplied by the user, but the user's reasoning was 'last known information before Reanimate was cast'. That is not the mechanism: last known information is only used for an object that has already left its zone (608.2h), and the Troll hasn't left the graveyard yet when the replacement effect applies; the count isn't locked in at cast time. The answer should NOT credit last known information or cast time. Key card ruling the answer should use: Golgari Grave-Troll 2018-12-07 ('If you return Golgari Grave-Troll from your graveyard directly to the battlefield, its first ability counts itself.'). Not located: a single CR rule that states the card is still in the graveyard at the moment 'enters with' is evaluated; the 'another creature card in response' sentence is my inference from 614.1 and 608.2h, please confirm or remove. Question text fixed from 'careature' to 'creature'.

question: If you cast Reckless Charge on Crag Puca, then activate Crag Puca's ability to switch its power and toughness, what will be the resulting power/toughness of Crag Puca?
expected_answer: 4/5. Crag Puca is a 2/4. Reckless Charge's +3/+0 applies in layer 7c, making it 5/4. Effects that switch power and toughness apply afterward in layer 7d, so the switch takes the 5/4 and makes it 4/5. The switch always applies after every other power/toughness effect regardless of which happened first, so activating the ability before casting Reckless Charge gives the same result.
notes: Answer supplied by the user. The question doesn't give Crag Puca's base stats, so the app has to look them up (2/4, from Scryfall). Writing this entry exposed a real gap: the cards table didn't store power/toughness/loyalty/defense, so lookup_card couldn't have returned them. Fixed in the same change (new columns, re-ingest, lookup_card output). Key card ruling the answer can use: Crag Puca 2021-03-19 ('Effects that switch a creature's power and toughness apply after all other effects, regardless of when those effects began to apply').

question: If I have Underworld Breach and my commander in play, can I escape Fierce Guardianship from my graveyard by exiling 3 cards and not paying its mana cost?
expected_answer: No. Underworld Breach gives Fierce Guardianship escape while it's in your graveyard, and casting it from the graveyard is only possible through that escape permission. Escape means you cast the card by paying its escape cost rather than its mana cost (702.138a), so it is an alternative cost. Fierce Guardianship's 'you may cast this spell without paying its mana cost' is also an alternative cost (118.9). Only one alternative cost can be applied to a spell as it's cast (118.9a, 601.2b), so you can't combine them. You can still escape it, but you pay the escape cost: its normal mana cost ({2}{U}) plus exiling three other cards from your graveyard. Controlling a commander doesn't make the mana part free in that case.
notes: Answer supplied by the user; rules found by Claude. The answer is correct. Details added by Claude, please confirm: (1) the point that Fierce Guardianship's own text gives no permission to cast it from the graveyard, so escape is the only way it can be cast from there. This is why you can't just cast it for free. (2) the escape cost under Underworld Breach is the card's mana cost plus exiling three other cards, so 'exiling 3 cards and not paying its mana cost' misreads the cost (the mana cost is still paid). Key card rulings the answer can use: Underworld Breach 2020-01-24 ('If you cast a spell with its escape permission, you can't choose to apply any other alternative costs or to cast it without paying its mana cost') and Fierce Guardianship 2020-04-17 (any commander counts). Question wording lightly edited for clarity.

question: What happens to Urza's Saga on chapter 2 when someone plays Blood Moon? Assume Blood Moon arrives after the chapter II ability has already resolved.
expected_answer: Blood Moon makes Urza's Saga a Mountain, a type-changing effect that applies in layer 4 (613.1d). Because the effect sets its land type to a basic land type, the land loses its old land type (Urza's) and all abilities generated from its rules text, which includes its chapter abilities, and it gains '{T}: Add {R}' (305.7). With no chapter abilities, the Saga stops receiving lore counters (714.3c) and the sacrifice state-based action no longer applies, since it only checks a Saga with one or more chapter abilities (704.5s). So it is not sacrificed after chapter III and stays on the battlefield as an enchantment land Mountain. It keeps the abilities it was granted by chapter abilities that already resolved: 305.7 says setting a land's subtype doesn't remove abilities granted by other effects, and those ability-adding effects apply in layer 6 (613.1f), after Blood Moon's layer 4 effect. Per the official Urza's Saga ruling, it keeps them for as long as it's on the battlefield. That means it keeps both '{T}: Add {C}' from chapter I and '{2}, {T}: Create a Construct' from chapter II, in addition to the Mountain's '{T}: Add {R}'.
notes: Answer supplied by the user; Claude added or changed several things, please confirm: (1) the rule that actually protects the granted abilities is 305.7 ('this doesn't remove any abilities that were granted to the land by other effects'). The layer ordering (layer 4 then layer 6) is consistent with it, but a different-layer argument alone isn't the stated reason. Your must_cite of 613.1d and 613.1f is kept, with 305.7 and 704.5s added. (2) 'Loses the ability to add lore counters' is true in effect, but the counter is added by a turn-based action (714.3c), not by a Saga ability. It simply doesn't apply to a Saga without chapter abilities. (3) Timing is fixed by the user: Blood Moon arrives after chapter II has already resolved, so both granted abilities are kept. Other timings would give different results (Blood Moon in play before the lore counter is added means chapter II never triggers; Blood Moon while chapter II's trigger is on the stack still lets the trigger resolve independently of its source, 113.7a), but they are not what this question asks. (4) Saga is an enchantment subtype, so I assume it stays an Enchantment Land, but I could not locate a rule that says so in as many words. Not mentioned in the CR: whether it's still a 'Saga' for other effects. Key card rulings the answer can use: Urza's Saga 2021-06-18 ('keeps those abilities for as long as it's on the battlefield') and Blood Moon 2020-08-07 ('Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had').

question: If I have Dryad of the Ilysian Grove in play, and one of my opponents plays Curious Colossus targeting me, does the Dryad stop applying its "Lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types" effect?
expected_answer: No, your lands stay every basic land type. Curious Colossus's enters trigger makes each creature the targeted player controls lose all abilities, which includes the Dryad, and become a 1/1 Coward. But the Dryad's land-type effect is a type-changing effect applied in layer 4 (613.1d), and the ability removal is applied later in layer 6 (613.1f). Layers are applied in order (613.1), so the Dryad's effect has already been applied by the time it loses its abilities, and removing the ability in layer 6 doesn't undo it. The lands keep the added land types and the matching mana abilities. The Dryad's other ability, 'You may play an additional land on each of your turns', does stop working, because the Dryad no longer has that ability.
notes: Answer supplied by the user, with must_cite 613.6. The conclusion (No) is right, but I think 613.6 is not the rule that gets you there, so I moved it to may_cite and made 613.1d and 613.1f the must_cite. Please confirm or tell me to put 613.6 back. Reasoning: 613.6 covers one effect that has parts in more than one layer (its examples are 'becomes the color of your choice and gets +1/+1' and Act of Treason's control change plus haste). It says the later parts keep applying to the same objects even if the ability generating the effect is removed. The Dryad's land-type effect only has one part, in layer 4, so there's no later layer for 613.6 to carry it into. What protects it is the layer order: layer 4 is applied before layer 6, so the Dryad still has the ability when layer 4 is applied. I could not find a CR rule that says this in so many words, only the layer list (613.1) and 613.5, so the 'removing the ability doesn't undo earlier layers' sentence is an inference from the order of the layers. Details added by Claude, please confirm: (1) the question now says Colossus targets you, since its trigger only affects creatures controlled by the target opponent (611.2c). Without that the Dryad isn't affected at all. (2) The Dryad's additional-land-play ability does stop working, as noted in the answer. The Colossus rulings include 2025-11-17 ('effects last indefinitely'). Neither card's rulings address this exact pairing.
